tagline.text: Climbing the Philippines' northernmost active volcano on Batan Island

location.label: Location
location.text: Basco, Batan Island, Batanes (trail starts at Sitio Banaraw near Basco Airport)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–June and clear days in September

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,000 (guide and transfer, per group; the ₱405 Batanes visitor registration is separate)

children.text: Mount Iraya is a stratovolcano rising

right beside Basco on Batan Island and is the northernmost active volcano in the Philippines. The day hike starts near Basco Airport, climbs through forest and a reed ridge, and rewards you with views over both the Pacific Ocean and the South China Sea.
Mount Iraya stands on Batan Island, the island of Batanes province in the Luzon Strait where the capital, Basco, is located. It is a stratovolcano about
high with a base roughly
5.5 km

across. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) still classifies it as active, and it is known as the northernmost active volcano in the country. Its last recorded eruption is said to have been in 1454. Beside Iraya sits Mount Matarem, a lower volcanic edifice, and together the two shape the volcanic landscape of northern Batan. The area belongs to the Luzon Volcanic Arc and the Pacific Ring of Fire, and the fertile volcanic soil has long supported farming and grazing on the lower slopes.

You can see the mountain from almost anywhere on the island, so Iraya is always in view from Basco town. To the Ivatan people it is a protective mother mountain, and a ring of cloud around the summit is said to be a sign that an elder in the community will soon pass away. It is best to climb quietly, as if entering a sacred place. In 1998 a swarm of earthquakes led to a temporary monitoring network, and today the Basco Seismological Station keeps watching the volcano. Check the latest PHIVOLCS announcements on volcanic activity.

The hike begins on a village road at Sitio Banaraw, right beside Basco Airport. The first 30 minutes or so are a breathless climb, followed by about 1.5 hours of dense forest filled with birdsong. Past the forest, on the shoulder ridge, tall reeds cover the path, and the last 30–45 minutes is a steep scramble pulling yourself up by the reeds. Even hikers used to big mountains say the mud and humidity make it harder than expected.

The summit is often wrapped in cloud, but when it clears you can see the Pacific Ocean to the east, Itbayat and Dinem Islands to the northwest, the South China Sea to the west, and Mount Matarem and Sabtang Island to the southwest, all at once. Waiting for the few minutes when the clouds open is part of the hike. There are no maintained trails, signposts or shops as on mountains near Seoul, so plan to climb with a guide. The upside is that few people go, and the birdsong in the forest and the wind sweeping through the reeds stay with you long afterward.

blocks.title: Northernmost active volcano in the Philippines

children.text: Iraya is a stratovolcano classified as active by PHIVOLCS,
high with a base about
5.5 km
wide. It is also the highest mountain in Batanes, and from the top the whole island lies below you.
The forest trail at the start has a variety of plants and birds, and above the shoulder ridge you enter a stand of tall reeds. Locally called vyawo, these reeds serve as handholds on the final climb.

On a clear day you can see the Pacific Ocean, the South China Sea, Itbayat and Dinem Islands, and Mount Matarem and Sabtang Island to the southwest of Batan. A strong, cool wind blows at the summit and dries your sweat.

blocks.title: Starts beside the airport, done in a day

children.text: The trailhead at Sitio Banaraw is right near Basco Airport, so it is a short guide-vehicle ride from your lodging. Start at dawn and you can be back early in the afternoon on a single-day hike.

blocks.title: A sacred mountain for the Ivatan

children.text: The Ivatan regard Iraya as a protective mother mountain. Climbing with a guide and hearing the stories about the mountain changes how the landscape looks. When you see clouds ringing the summit, it is easy to understand why the mountain has been considered sacred.

Mountaineering guides say that around September, the so-called mini-summer, there is less cloud and the views are most likely to be good. Wind direction is another hint: locals say a north wind brings cloud and an east wind clears the sky.
If the climb feels like too much, photographing Iraya's ridgeline from places such as Tukon Church or the Basco Lighthouse hill is impressive enough.

items.title: One-day climb
items.subtitle: Leave at dawn, descend in the afternoon

children.text: Meet your guide at your lodging and head to the entrance of Sitio Banaraw. Check your water, snacks, spare socks and rain gear.
Start the hike from the trailhead near Basco Airport. The first
30 minutes
are a steep climb, so set a slow pace.
Rest once at the edge of the forest, then enter the dense forest trail. The forest continues for about
1.5 hours
, and after rain it is very muddy.
Reach the shoulder ridge (a viewpoint that can also serve as a campsite). The trees disappear and the reed fields begin.
Climb the last stretch holding on to the reeds. It takes about
30–45 minutes
Arrive at the summit ridge, wait for the clouds to clear, take photos and have a snack.
Begin the descent. The mud makes it more slippery than on the way up, so protect your knees and ankles.
Back at the trailhead, return to your lodging and finish with pancit Cabagan or halo-halo in town.

The timetable above is based on a sample from a mountaineering information site. Depending on fitness and weather, the summit can take 3–4 hours and the descent about 3 hours, so leave some margin. The day before, agree with your guide on the start time, the cancellation rule in rain, and what the fee includes (transfer, meals, water), so you are not scrambling at dawn.

items.title: A day in Basco plus views
items.subtitle: Enjoying Iraya without climbing

children.text: Walk around the morning market and the church in Basco town with Iraya as the backdrop.
Head to a hilltop viewpoint and enjoy the scenery where Iraya's ridge and the sea appear together.
On a clear day, take photos in the afternoon light when Iraya's slopes stand out most clearly.
Rules on climbing permits and guides can change, so check the latest guidance with your lodging or the tourism office.
The Philippine Airlines (PAL) direct Manila–Basco route ended on 25 October 2025; PAL Express now flies from Clark (CRK) to Basco Airport (BSO). The flight from Clark takes about
1 hour 15 minutes
, and getting from Manila to Clark by road adds roughly 2–3 hours. Flight days and frequency can change, so check the latest PAL announcements.

Besides PAL Express (Clark route), Basco Airport is known to be served by Sky Pasada (Tuguegarao, Laoag, Calayan and others) and Fliteline Airways (Itbayat, Tuguegarao), so if Clark does not suit you, look into routes via Tuguegarao or Laoag.
Flights to Batanes have few seats and sell out quickly during holidays and the summer. It is best to book early.

items.title: From the airport to the trailhead

children.text: The trailhead at Sitio Banaraw is very close to Basco Airport, and you can get there from Basco town by a short tricycle ride.
When you hire a guide, the transfer from your lodging to the trailhead is often included, so ask when you book.
Some accounts describe the trailhead as within walking distance of the airport, but considering luggage and the heat, a tricycle or your lodging's vehicle is more comfortable.

Reports say Batanes has required advance visitor registration since June 15, 2026: ₱405 per person (₱200 ecotourism fee plus ₱205 visitor ID), paid online, after which you receive a QR code. Rules may change, so check the latest announcement on the official portal.
Registration asks you to name a Department of Tourism (DOT) accredited tour operator, so it helps to settle your lodging and guide beforehand.
Iraya is a damp mountain, so expect cloud and mud in any season, but the best visibility is known to come in September, the so-called mini-summer with less cloud. Basco gets about
of rain a year on average, which is plentiful, and the humidity is high.

During typhoon season flights and boats are often cut off, so leave some slack in your schedule. Locals say a north wind brings cloud and an east wind opens the sky, so ask your guide about the wind the day before.

Homestays and small hotels cluster in Basco town and around the airport, which makes them convenient for the night before the hike. Iraya is close to Basco, so even if you stay in another town you can do it as a day trip. Lodgings often arrange the guide. Batanes is an island, so prices tend to be higher than on the mainland and restaurants keep short hours; it helps to decide in advance where you will eat dinner the night before and lunch the next day.

After the hike, pancit Cabagan and halo-halo at a town panciteria are described as the classic finish for hikers. There are no convenience stores on the mountain, so prepare water and lunch before you start.
Meet your guide at 6 a.m. and start early to avoid the afternoon cloud and heat.
Bring shoes with good grip, gloves and a change of socks. Sandals are dangerous.
Wear a quick-drying long-sleeved shirt and bring rain gear. The reeds and thorns scratch easily.
Bring plenty of water, ideally in a hydration bag, and pack lunch. No water source on the mountain has been confirmed.
Mobile signal reaches near the summit, but uploads can be slow. Bring a power bank.
Many reports say the descent is more slippery than the climb, so trekking poles help.
Wait 20–30 minutes at the summit for the clouds to open. Sometimes the sky clears after you leave.
To split the guide fee, you can also join other travelers climbing the same day.
Bring a plastic bag for wet shoes and clothes after the hike to keep your lodging and the transfer vehicle clean.

Iraya is an active volcano monitored by PHIVOLCS, and its slopes fall inside a protected area. Under local government rules, visitors to protected areas are sometimes required to be accompanied by a DENR-accredited guide, so be sure to check the latest rules with the tourism office or your lodging before you set out.
Mud and wet roots make slips likely, and the descent is riskier. Watch your knees and ankles.
Low branches and vines can hit your head or catch your ankles. Keep your eyes ahead in the forest.
Snakes are said to live in the forest but are reported to be non-venomous. Still, do not put your hands down carelessly.
Cloud and rain at the summit can chill you, so bring a windproof layer.
Permit procedures and fees differ between sources and are hard to pin down. Be sure to confirm the latest information locally.
Travel information for the whole province where Iraya is located. You can plan an itinerary combining Batan, Sabtang and Itbayat islands.
An island visible to the southwest from the summit of Iraya on a clear day; you can cross by boat to see its stone-house villages.
A viewpoint hill close to Basco town from which you can see Iraya's ridgeline in the distance.
